In 14 years of gastroenterology practice, I’ve treated over 2,000 patients on GLP-1 medications — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound.

And I’ll tell you what I tell every single one of them on their first visit: **the digestive problems you’re experiencing are not ‘just side effects.’ They’re a predictable consequence of what these medications do to your stomach — and there’s a reason nothing you’ve tried has worked.**

Not the Miralax. Not the fiber. Not the ginger chews. Not even the prescription Zofran your doctor called in.

Because every single one of those remedies is aimed at the wrong organ.

## Every Laxative You’ve Tried Was Aimed at the Wrong Organ

Here’s what’s actually happening inside your body:

GLP-1 medications work by slowing your stomach. That’s the mechanism — slower gastric emptying means you feel full longer, eat less, lose weight. It’s brilliant pharmacology.

But when the stomach slows _too much_, a feedback loop kicks in:

**1\. Food sits in the stomach too long** → fermentation begins → hydrogen sulfide gas builds up (that’s your sulfur burps).

**2\. The distension from gas and undigested food** → triggers more slowing → the stomach essentially goes into “park.”

**3\. Nothing moves downstream** → constipation sets in. Not because the colon is broken — because nothing is reaching it.

This is why Miralax doesn’t work. Miralax pulls water into the colon. But if nothing is reaching the colon in the first place, you’re just hydrating an empty pipe. Same with Dulcolax, Metamucil, even enemas — they’re all **downstream solutions for an upstream problem.**

The problem is in your _stomach_. The solution needs to start there too.

## The Three-Pathway Protocol I Now Put Every GLP-1 Patient On

![advertorial adv 3](https://www.getmotilli.com/cdn/shop/files/advertorial-adv-3.jpg?v=1774542931&width=1200)

After years of watching patients cycle through laxatives, I developed a protocol that addresses all three pathways of GLP-1 digestive dysfunction simultaneously:

**Pathway 1: Gastric Motility (The Stomach Wake-Up)**

Celery juice concentrate contains **apigenin** — a natural prokinetic compound that stimulates the vagus nerve, which controls stomach muscle contractions. Instead of forcing movement from below, it gently nudges the stomach to do what it’s designed to do: move food through. Think of it as physical therapy for a muscle that’s been put to sleep by the medication.

**Pathway 2: Sulfur Gas Neutralization (The Odor Fix)**

**Chlorophyllin** directly binds to hydrogen sulfide molecules — the compound responsible for sulfur burps. It doesn’t mask the smell. It chemically neutralizes the gas before it can travel up your esophagus. Most patients report dramatic improvement within 48–72 hours.

**Pathway 3: Gentle Lubrication, Not Bulk (The Regularity Solution)**

**Soluble prebiotic fiber** in micro-doses works completely differently from Metamucil or psyllium. Instead of adding bulk to an already-backed-up system, it lubricates the intestinal lining and feeds beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids — natural compounds that stimulate gentle, rhythmic contractions. No cramping. No urgency. Just quiet, predictable regularity.

## Why I Recommend Motilli Specifically

I don’t make a habit of endorsing specific supplements. But after two years of watching my GLP-1 patients struggle, I started recommending Motilli for four specific reasons:

**1\. It targets the stomach, not the colon.** Most digestive supplements work downstream. Motilli’s celery juice extract works upstream — where the problem actually is.

**2\. It addresses all three pathways simultaneously.** Motility, sulfur gas, and gentle regularity — in one product. No more juggling 5–6 bottles.

**3\. The gummy format matters.** My patients with GLP-1 nausea can’t swallow large capsules. Motilli’s pectin-based gummies melt in your mouth and are gentle on sensitive stomachs.

**4\. No prescription required, no dose changes needed.** It works alongside your GLP-1 medication, not against it. You don’t have to reduce your dose or add another prescription.

I’ll put it simply: **it’s what I give my own mother.** She started Mounjaro eight months ago. The constipation was brutal. I put her on Motilli, and within a week she was calling me to say “whatever you gave me — don’t let me run out.”
